utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made still applies of course. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated yesterday that you did not attend the talks at Rambouillet. Did you attend the talks later on in March in Paris?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your assessment of those or of what transpired at those two venues comes from the reports you received from the FRY and Serbian delegation, particularly Mr. Sainovic and Dr. -- or Professor Markovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was your -- or from where did you get your information on what transpired at those two meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally drafted an analysis of all the texts which followed from Rambouillet and Paris. I read them in the English original, and this is how I got the gist of the process. And on the other hand, as is known, I had a large team of diplomats and technical staff who followed on a constant basis all the activities at Rambouillet and Paris, and they briefed me through the Paris embassy on the course of negotiations on a daily basis, virtually on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Well, did you receive reports from Mr. Sainovic and Professor Markovic at all?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall them informing the ministry about the results and the course of the activities at Rambouillet and Paris --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay, very well --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but because I was just a minister in that government. Mr. Sainovic was the vice-president of the federal government, and Mr. Markovic was the vice-president of the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we briefly look at P398, I think it is. I think it's P1151, I'm sorry. It will come up on your screen, Mr. Markovic [sic].

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Do I have this document in my binder or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this binder of any use at all now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It possibly might be.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm asking because I have technical difficulties approaching the -- this screen. If I can have a hard copy, it's much easier for me than watching things on the screen. I'm of poor sight, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My apologies to the Registrar. It's P1513.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Jovanovic, I don't have a hard copy, but it is one page, and I'll have it brought up to a bigger picture if possible. And I think it's a pretty straightforward document. This is a letter of the 26th of March from the former Prosecutor of this Tribunal, Louise Arbour, and it's just at the onset of the NATO intervention, and it is addressed to President Milosevic. If you could quickly familiarise yourself with the contents of the letter.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall -- I believe this letter would have been sent through diplomatic channels. Do you recall seeing and -- well, seeing this letter at or about the time when it was sent?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall this letter. May I remind esteemed, Mr. Prosecutor, that this goes to the relationship between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. And in the legal system of the time, Yugoslavia's relations with The Hague Tribunal were within the exclusive remit of the federal justice ministry. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs does not have any particular competences in this regard even today. This matter is managed by the National Council for the co-operation with the Tribunal or some such body. So at the time this letter were written and today Serbia's relations with the Tribunal were never within the remit of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards -- as regards the competence of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, back at the time when I was minister and today, those competencies are precisely laid down in the foreign affairs law which is still in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you in your meetings that you had with the leadership of the FRY and Serbia discuss or know of any discussions of the contents of this letter or of the grave concerns expressed by the Prosecutrix at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that. I do not recall the content of this letter being discussed at any meeting that I attended. As I've already stated, matters of this kind were either within the exclusive competence of the Ministry of Justice, and there is ample state documentation about this, including the correspondence between the Ministry of Justice with the OTP and other UN agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- well, let me clarify something. Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic, the minister of justice -- sorry, not justice, the minister of the MUP, the minister of interior, was also a leading member of the party like yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic may have been for a time in the top leadership of the SPS, but I'm not familiar with that fact. For years of the SPS's existence I held diplomatic posts abroad, meaning outside the country, but while I was vice chairman of the party in charge of international relations, I do not recall that Mr. Stojiljkovic had any elevated position. It's possible that he might have been a member of a committee which numbered more than 350 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you during the -- or during 1999 participate in any meeting where Mr. Stojiljkovic was present?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but that question is very vague. Do you mean any meeting with -- over 365 days in a year? Could you be more specific, please. I must point out, as a rule Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic as minister of the interior of Serbia and yours truly as the federal minister for foreign affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia chanced upon each other extremely rarely and even less rarely did we attend the same meetings. We held posts at different levels. He held a republican post, and I was a member of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. So I presume, since you are -- chanced upon each other very rarely, as you put it, that you recall if you met or if you participated in meetings that he participated in. And I'll be more precise. Let's just talk about meetings relating to affairs in Kosovo. Did you at any level, whether federal or republican, participate in any meetings with Mr. Stojiljkovic in respect of matters relating to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall - and I'm moving on to something else, Mr. Jovanovic - meeting with the High Commissioner for -- the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mary Robinson, in 1999 during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, it doesn't seem right that I see some documents for the first time as the one before this, that I had no opportunity to see before entering this courtroom. And the document being announced now is something I did not see. For instance, the last document, although not very long, requires that I get familiar with it in advance, at least a bit in advance, so that I can be of use as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did attend more than one meeting with Madam Robinson. I cannot recall exactly how many there were, but at least there were two meetings. I recall one meeting with her at the New York headquarters of the UN. We attended a working breakfast together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in September, but I'm not sure whether it was in 1998 or 1999, because in September of 1998 and in September of 1999 I went to the UN and I met her at one of the General Assembly meetings and had a working breakfast with her. And it's true, she did visit Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm talking about. Did she visit Belgrade in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me right, yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did she tell you that in her capacity as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, she had received reports that there was a campaign of ethnic cleansing - to use the word then in general parlance - being conducted against the Kosovar Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall all the issues that we discussed in any degree or detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up 65 ter 06019.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a UN HCHR press release of the 13th of May, 1999, and I probably don't need to read this into the record. Can you read the first four paragraphs, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see only two paragraphs on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you're through reading them, we'll scroll down. You could just let us know when you're through.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read those first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I read the remaining text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, firstly, do you recall that when she visited Belgrade, she met and spoke with you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a time of war. There were many such visits. She did visit, but I cannot recall specifically the time. But yes, we did hold talks in Belgrade. I see that this is a press release. I'm sure that the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Yugoslavia issued its own communique about that, but I do not have it with me at that if I may say so my communique or press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: According to the UN HRCR release, she complained to you or told you that she had received accounts given by hundreds of Kosovar Albanian refugees about a campaign of ethnic cleansing carried out by the army and police and paramilitary forces. Do you recall her telling you that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall such an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall her telling you anything at all about Kosovar Albanian refugees? After all, she was the High Commissioner for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but unfortunately I must say that I do not recall almost any issues that we discussed, apart from -- in principle the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights was interested in the state of human rights in the area of Yugoslavia, including Kosovo. But I personally cannot recall in any degree of detail any issue or any intervention that may be akin to that statement that she provided at a press conference in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, can you recall having any discussion with her about any matter having to do with human rights?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, today, 11 years after the meeting, the only thing I can say is that at that meeting we discussed human rights, but I cannot be any more specific about which issues, which matters, which terms were used by Madam Robinson, which assessment she uttered, either talking to me or at the press conference. This is something that I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this is a quote from Mrs. Robinson, and I'll just read it. She said: "Justice must be done. I am determined that there will be accountability and that we will break the cycle of impunity. The similarities between Kosovo and Bosnia should not include suspected war criminals walking around freely after a settlement is reached." Now, surely you must remember that statement, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you assist him, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have to recall. I have already said that I do not remember, and in any case, this is a statement by Madam Robinson at a press conference, not something that she said to me personally. So I really cannot recall whether anybody published or whether this was published or not. In any event, I can agree with Madam Robinson, with her statement, at the press conference that justice must prevail. Yes, of course, justice must prevail. I agree with that statement by Madam Robinson given at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Whatever it is that Madam -- or Mrs. Robinson told you about the human rights situation in Kosovo -- and I understand that you say you don't recall what she told you, but can I take it that you would have communicated what she said to the relevant government department, that is, the MUP and the defence department responsible for the army?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Each one of my conversations with foreign representatives, particularly such a high-ranking representative from the UN system, is something that I would inform the federal government about, and then the federal government made the decision as to whom they would convey the contents and to whom they would issue certain instructions so that certain things could be resolved. I am seeing this text for the first time. I didn't have time to check back what my ministry did in relation to the federal government and other institutions of the system, but I can state with a high degree of certainty that a report was made on this and pursuant to the usual practice, it was submitted to the federal government and other authorised bodies, for them to act further upon the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, before I sit, Your Honours, could this document be received in evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin my cross-examination, I would like to make an objection to providing documents after the examination-in-chief of the witness has begun. We received six or seven documents yesterday, and as for this document, I think I received it the day before yesterday during the examination-in-chief. And I think yesterday I received this letter by Madam Louise Arbour. I would like to ask the Prosecution not to make this a practice, this type of behaviour, because that puts us at a disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, and to counsel. There was a problem in our review, the research system, last week, which we have overcome. And we will not make it a practice, but I accept that we did not have the facility to find these documents until very late, and we disclosed them to the Defence immediately upon doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. You will well appreciate that the efficiency with which we proceed and the completeness and reliability of anything a witness may say about a document will be adversely affected if that document is not known to the witness before giving evidence. Our procedures will work far better if the witness has had a time to reflect upon documents before giving evidence. Mr. Djurdjic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Although you've already responded, did the Ministry of Foreign Affairs ever receive this document or any kind of press release, as it is stated here, by the High Commissioner from the 17th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, this is something that one would not receive, just like other regular mail. It's something that would be read in the media, and all that the ministry would receive would be a bunch of documents. So the minister would not really have access, other than the things that were directly addressed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, having in mind the gravity of what is stated here as being told to you as serious violations of human rights in Kosovo, would it be usual in diplomatic practice to provide such statements in the form of a note and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be usual. We had an example earlier of a letter by Madam Arbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive a note during the aggression on the FRY or the Republic of Serbia in 1999 that had to do with violations of human rights in Kosovo and Metohija and crimes by the FRY and Serbian security forces?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't receive such protests, either in the form of notes or written interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that Madam Mary Robinson informed you about this in a conversation and that you would then not remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, we can conclude very clearly from the text that this was a statement by Madam Robinson given at a press conference. In conversations between high-ranking government representatives and representatives of other international legal subjects, legal entities, one would very infrequently encounter such phrases that were used in the statement to the press, that we had the opportunity to see today for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had something like that been said to you in the talks, in this manner or in a less forceful manner, would you have reacted?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this is a dialogue that we're talking about, and I would like to remind you that analysis by the federal government and the republican Government of Serbia indicated that the terrorist KLA forced its compatriots to leave their settlements in order to create the appearance of a humanitarian catastrophe in order to justify the NATO aggression. This doesn't mean that there were no individual crimes committed by persons from all over the place, but that does not also mean that the state conducted any kind of policy of persecution, ethnic cleansing, or mass violence, as it is more or less stated in the text that we had the opportunity to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jovanovic, Mr. Stamp showed you yesterday on page 56, lines 1 to 3, your statement from the Milutinovic transcript where you stated that Kertes gave you money, amongst other things, for the reconstruction of the diplomatic offices. You stated so in the Milutinovic case. I'm asking you whether the embassy of China is a diplomatic premise?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So could you please tell me why the Chinese spent over 470.000 German marks for repairs of their embassy?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal government, first of all, assigned or allocated a building for their use. If I remember correctly, this was to be used by the consulate. The building was dilapidated when it was handed over, so in order to make it fit for use, it was necessary to make a significant investment, which the federal government was not able to cover because the budget had a deficit. So there was an agreement reached with the Chinese side that they should do the repairs of the building with their own funds, the building that they were going to use, and then the Yugoslav side would compensate for these funds over a longer period of time by waiving the rent. After the agreement was reached, for the Chinese embassy to leave the restored building before the waived rents would be able to cover the entire amount that was invested in order to repair the building, the condition for vacation was a difference of some 475.000, which was supposed to be paid to the Chinese side so that the accounts would be settled in terms of what they invested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But just tell me, when you were talking about the expenses for the diplomatic offices, which ones were you actually thinking of?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the embassy of the People's Republic of China.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On this last issue, Mr. Jovanovic, are you saying that the federal government in effect provided the embassy premises for a foreign government in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in two ways: Either as property or property to be rented. In the first case it was on the basis of reciprocity and in the second case it was as-needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was this a normal diplomatic arrangement in the federal government's dealing with other nations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Pursuant to the convention on diplomatic relations and diplomatic practice, the universal rule is to provide buildings for foreign diplomatic representatives on the basis of reciprocity. If one country should hand over to another country their property in order to be used for diplomatic purposes, it is assumed that the other country would also provide a premises to them in turn for their embassy. It's not so in every single case, but depending on the relations and the legal systems, this is the case in the vast majority of cases throughout the world. Lesser degree -- to a lesser degree, these matters are resolved by providing buildings for rent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add a question. Why was this money transferred in cash?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for a considerable period of time was subject to sanctions, so the financial payment system did not function internationally. No money practically could be transferred through the usual banking channels. Your Honour, during the period of the sanctions, the entire Yugoslav diplomatic corps was financed by having cash brought and distributed to the embassies. You can imagine what an effort this was if one keeps in mind that Yugoslavia had diplomatic relations with 178 countries and that it had over 100 embassies and consulates throughout the world. Each one had to be given money in cash during the period of the sanctions, and this cash had to be obtained or provided by the federal ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I want to direct your mind to evidence you gave on the 25th of January in answer to Defence counsel. He asked you a particular question. "The measures undertaken in Kosovo and Metohija, were they directed against people who were not engaging in terrorism, irrespective of their ethnic background?" Do you recollect this question being asked of you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the government measures were directed primarily at terrorists, exclusively against terrorists and elements that used violence in order to achieve their political goals. The measures were not aimed against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Well, you see, I just wanted to have it clear because you answered: "Of course." So I imagine you meant "of course not."

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful to you for this intervention because evidently it was not properly stated or was inadequately entered into the transcript, but it is quite clear that the measures by the organs of authority were not directed against the civilian population but against elements and the organisations which used terrorism and violence in order to achieve their political goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. And this you can verify as a fact, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can confirm this as the policy of the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whose foreign minister I was. The policy of the federal government and the policy of the Government of the Republic of Serbia was to secure at any cost a peaceful political solution and compromise with respect of the UN resolutions and the Helsinki Final Act, as well as with respect of the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity. So in that sense, Your Honour, there were no obstacles to Yugoslavia to even accept a political solution in Paris. Yugoslavia and Serbia were not able to accept secession and the breaking away of Kosovo and Metohija. This is where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, there's just one small point I shall like you to clarify for me, just one more. Now, in some areas of your evidence in answer to Defence counsel you referred to the Albanian ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, were the Albanians always in the minority?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanians were always a minority outside of their home state of Albania. Albanians as a ethnic minority mostly lived in Serbia, then in Macedonia where percentage-wise in relation to the total population of Macedonia there are many more Albanians than this percentage in Serbia. There are also Albanians living in Greece and in Montenegro, and in all these countries they live as a national minority. Why a national minority? Because pursuant to the Convention of the Council of Europe on the rights of members of ethnic minorities, there are homeland states, parent states, and so the person who does not live in their parent states, who lives in another country, would enjoy the status of an ethnic minority in that country. This is a legal term that is absolutely respected in the Council of Europe Convention on respect for the rights of national minorities. Thus, Your Honour, there are more than 1 million Albanians in Kosovo. There has been no census there for quite some time, so this is not a reliable figure, but regardless of this number, over 1 million citizens, in Serbia they are an ethnic minority. They are not an ethnic minority only in Albania. In all the other neighbouring countries, the Albanians are an ethnic minority and, Your Honour, they enjoy the rights arising from the Convention of the Council of Europe, which include many rights in terms of their culture, education, history, identity. But the rights of members of national minorities do not anywhere include the right to secession --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the right to self-determination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Jovanovic, you'll be pleased to know that ends the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here and for the assistance you've been able to give us, and you are now of course free to go back to your normal activities. And an officer of the Court will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our witness is ready. I don't know if it would be better to take a break now and then to continue, or do you think we should continue with our new witness? Mr. Aleksandar Popovic will be examining the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have over half an hour to the normal break. I think we could call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. I believe Mr. Popovic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, before I start my examination, I would like to ask you, since we speak the same language, after hearing my question make a pause to allow the interpreters to finish interpreting my question and then to start interpreting your answer. Please state your name.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Radomir Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of February, 1943, in the Sekiraca village of the municipality of Kursumlija, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gojovic, did you testify before this court in the Milutinovic trial on the 2nd and 3rd of October --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- in 2007? During the proofing session, did you have an opportunity to read through what you testified about in the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you would like to make certain corrections and to explain and clarify some of your answers recorded in the transcripts of your testimony in the Milutinovic case. Now I would like to allow you to do that. And for the benefit of my learned friends and Their Honours, I would like to point out that in the Milutinovic transcript on page 16764, line 25, and on page 16765, lines 1 to 4, what is recorded there is the question of the Presiding [as interpreted] Judge Nosworthy about whether there was an obligation on the part of citizens to report a crime and the witness' answer to that question. Now I'm giving you an opportunity to clarify your answer that you provided then and to state it loud and clear here.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: A misunderstanding occurred then, and I overlooked something, and I would like to add to make it more precise and accurate. Each citizen, if learning that a criminal offence has been committed, punishable by death sentence, should report such an offence; failing that, he may be punished by three years in prison. This is a federal law provision and applies to military police officers, et cetera. So an official person which learns ex officio that a criminal offence has been committed punishable by five years in prison or more and fails to do so, then they may be punished by three years in prison and more. Which means all military officers when executing their duties has also the character of an official person. I overlooked this provision because we were discussing the Law on Military Officers, which regulates the question and the issue of such relations and obligations. And I believe that now I've clarified this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you've clarified this point, would you answer all the questions from the transcript, would you answer them in the same way that you did then during the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were no other reasons for me to say anything other than what I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document, 65 ter 1664. This would be the transcript of Witness Gojovic's testimony in the Milutinovic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00496.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to read out a summary of the witness statement of Mr. Gojovic. The witness is a lawyer who spent more than 40 years as member of the Yugoslav Army, before retiring with -- holding the rank of major in 2001. In his professional career, witness was the presiding judge of the military court in Belgrade from 1st of January, 1994, to the 16th of April, 1999, when he was appointed chief of the administration of the General Staff of -- the legal administration of the General Staff of the VJ. He is going to testify about the efforts he invested in improving the military legal system, inter alia, by within his remit providing all the necessary logistic support to the military justice system, and he requested and allowed the inclusion of the necessary professional personnel into the military justice system of the FRY and contributed to a normal functioning of the military justice system and the execution of its legal obligations and duties. The witness is going to discuss and explain the criminal procedure from detection to conviction or the final judgement. He is going to testify about the documents which the military handed out to all members of the VJ and about the training that members of the VJ undertook, particularly in respect of honouring international regulations and conventions, regulated the conduct during war and the respect for international humanitarian law. The witness is going to testify about the position, autonomy, and independence of the organs of the military justice system in relation to all the other organs, departments, and services of the General Staff of the VJ. In his testimony, he will particularly analyse information, reports, and overviews and summaries prepared for the use of the General Staff and for the VJ which contained reports about criminal offences perpetrated by the members of the VJ in Kosovo. He's going to talk about the number of criminal reports, the number of investigations conducted, the number of indictments, and the number of judgements in such proceedings. The witness is going to analyse orders issued by the General Staff of the VJ, who he -- which he personally drafted, which insisted on the need to detect crime and emphasized the obligation of all members of the VJ to respect the provisions of international humanitarian law. From his personal experience, he's going to confirm that if crimes were detected and reported, that they were all investigated and processed if there were grounds for -- to initiate proceedings. Thank you very much. That would be the summary of the witness' statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, were you a member of the VJ, and until what time if you were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I was member of the Yugoslav People's Army. I was an active officer from July 1961, and after that I was member of the VJ until the 1st of April, 2001, when I retired. Before that, I graduated from the military high school from 1959 to 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, when you retired, which rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I was major-general in the legal department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain your education.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the military high school, and after that I graduated from the grammar school and the law school in Sarajevo. Then I passed the bar examination and the examination for major, and I spent my whole career in the military justice system. In the meantime, I achieved a master's degree in Belgrade at the criminal law department of the law school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down when providing your answers. Could you please briefly explain to us which posts you held within the JNA and the VJ in your career.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from the military school, I stayed at that school as a commander and teacher of the cadets. After that I commanded a platoon until 1971. I was then promoted to the rank of lieutenant in the legal department, and I took up a post at the military court in Sarajevo. After trainership and after passing the bar exam, I was appointed deputy military prosecutor in Sarajevo. I spent four years there occupying that position. Then I was an investigative judge at the military court in Sarajevo for another four years. After that I was deputy military ombudsman and for another five years --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer -- the last portion of his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last section of --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The secretary of the military disciplinary tribunal and deputy of the public prosecutor at the command of the 7th Army in Sarajevo. After that I was president of a panel of judges for another three years at the same military court in Sarajevo. After that, deputy prosecutor -- military prosecutor in Sarajevo for another two years. Then for another three years, a military prosecutor in Sarajevo. After that, I was deputy military prosecutor general of the JNA for two years. After that, president of the military court in Belgrade from the 1st of January, 1994, until the 16th of April, 1999, more than four years. Then head of the general legal department of the General Staff from the 16th of April, 1999, and then head of the legal department of the Ministry of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So that would be all the posts within the legal profession, both as a clerk and as an officer or an official within that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After retiring in 2001, did you perform any tasks or were you involved or engaged by the VJ, its General Staff, or the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After retiring, there was a need at the time to establish co-operation between the Ministry of Defence and the VJ General Staff with this Tribunal. There were some requests concerning the delivery of documents and similar matters. And for that purpose, the minister of defence, in co-operation with the Chief of the General Staff, established a commission. It was labelled a Commission For the Co-Operation with The Hague Tribunal. I was asked to accept the post of deputy chairman of that commission as a professional, an expert, or a person who would facilitate the work of that commission. That commission worked for a period of three years. Later on, a different commission was established with different members.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us what the tasks of that commission was. Just briefly, if you remember, how many members did the commission have, and could you maybe name some of those permanent members. Very briefly, if you remember; if not, we will just carry on.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the commission had seven permanent members. The chairman of the commission was an active-duty general, Lieutenant-General Zlatoje Terzic, who was at the head of the training sector, military training sector. I was his deputy. And then there was also a representative from each sector of the ministry or the General Staff, so that there were a total of six or seven members. I was the only one who was retired. Also, Lieutenant-General Geza Farkas was retired. All the others were active-duty members of different ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will go back to 1999. If I understood you correctly, on the 16th of April, 1999, you were appointed as chief of the legal administration at the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the legal administration in the General Staff. There is a difference. When you say "in the General Staff" or "attached to the General Staff." If it's in the staff, then it's a part of the General Staff; if it's an organ that is attached to the General Staff, it's an independent organ, but that has some connection to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at that post?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until mid-2000, then I became the chief of the legal administration at the Ministry of Defence because those two administrations had merged. This was in order to stream-line our operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain a little more to us what the role and the function of the legal administration is in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia when you took on that post.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Its main task was to be a professional organ that dealt with all the legal matters for the needs of the General Staff, and the most important thing other than that was to organise and secure the functioning of military courts and military prosecutors during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you took up your duties on the 16th of April, 1999, what were the tasks that you were given, and what was the situation regarding the military courts and prosecutors' offices that you encountered when you took up your duties?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I would just before that like to say that with the declaration of the state of war on the 24th of March, 1999, and pursuant to the plan, the military courts and military prosecutors were activated in wartime. This function does not exist in peacetime. During wartime, the structure and the organisation of these bodies is quite different. So putting them into effect was something that was done for the first time after World War II, and in that sense there was a lack of experience and other knowledge as to how they would work in practice. There was a lot of theory, but of course, there is a lot of difference between theory and practice, particularly in the middle of a state of war. I was the president of the military army -- of the military court of the 1st Army. So on the 16th of April, a couple of days before that, we were organising and establishing these courts, getting them up to operate. So in the situation of these newly formed courts, of which there were 23 or 24, and of course there were the military prosecutors, the first difficulties and discrepancies began to appear between practice and what was assumed in theory. This was something that was noticed, of course. So there was a need for someone who had enough experience and knowledge in the profession to reorganise all of that in order to create a more favourable environment. The superiors thought that I, because I was one of the rare ones in the legal practice who had carried out all these duties, the prosecutor, the presiding of the panel of judges, I worked in commands outside of the courts, I worked in higher courts. So they believed that I had a lot of experience throughout my professional duties, and so they appointed me in order to improve the organisation and the functioning of the courts. And this is a complex matter, it's something that is evident here as well. In any kind of operation of the court there is a lot of logistical support required in order to meet the specific and quite considerable requirements that were set. So these were the reasons that guided my superiors to appoint me to this post.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you've given us a pretty exhaustive answer, so let us summarise. You, as an experienced professional in the legal field, were appointed to set up the legal bodies?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the legal and military bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the legal administration, what would be the relationship of the military administration within the General Staff in relation to the military courts and the military prosecutors' offices?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier that the legal administration is a professional organ in the General Staff in relation to the military courts and the military prosecutors who are independent and autonomous in their work. The legal administration is a link as a professional organ between the General Staff, their requirements in terms of uncovering and processing the perpetrators of crimes, and the military courts and the military prosecutors. So I was the link which on the one hand communicated with those organs and on the other hand, because the organisation is headed by a professional service of the General Staff, the legal administration is entrusted with all the tasks that had to do with the organisation and the formation of the wartime military tribunals at military staffs and units. So this is a unit that provided logistical personnel and professional support.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Still on this subject, let us now go back to the peacetime period. How were the military courts organised in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The military courts are organised in a completely different way in peacetime. During that period there were three military courts, three military prosecutors' offices at the first instance, and there was the supreme military court and the supreme military prosecutor as the institutions of second instance. The military court was seated in Belgrade. The lower military prosecutors' offices were also located in Belgrade as well as the higher court. There was also a lower military court in Nis and Podgorica, and they had prosecutors' offices there as well. They were appointed according to the territorial principles, so in specific territories. In wartime, these bodies are not formed according to the territorial principle but according to the personnel principle. They were attached to the unit commands. So they're only there in order to prosecute members of a specific command; that is why we had many more of them, 21 lower such courts and there were -- was one supreme military court with its four departments. And I can talk about them more specifically later. This is what the difference is. The lower military courts in peacetime cover all the territories that -- all the units that happen to be in that territory. So they prosecute the perpetrators of crimes from units which are located in the territory they're responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we now deal with this. You explained the functional and the actual jurisdiction of the peacetime courts. What changed with the proclamation of the state of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: With the declaration of the state of war - because these are completely different and more complex circumstances - the military justice organ -- organisation was adapted to these newly created circumstances, meaning that they are formed at the commands of specific units so that they encompass all the units that are established in wartime at a specific level. And the courts were then formed at the unit commands, the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Armies had these bodies; then the naval military command; the air force command also; the corps commands also had these bodies as well as the command of one division because this was an independent unit. So this is as far as the operational units are concerned. Then these bodies were formed at the military district commands too. Then the supreme military court was formed with its four departments, the headquarters of this court were in Belgrade, and the departments of the supreme military court were then at the army commands. Parallel with that, you had the same situation as far as the military prosecutor was concerned. The headquarters were in Belgrade at the General Staff, and its departments were located at the army commands. I mean, we can talk about the number of corps that there were, then the number of military districts. So then the system of military courts were adapted to the conditions so that they could be out there immediately in the field and could do their work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about numbers, you said that there were three military courts during peacetime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were during the war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: There were about 20 or 21 during the war. The lower courts and then we had one court of higher instance that had four departments which were dealing with appeals cases. And there was the same number of prosecutors, military prosecutors, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just one more question that will round off this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, let's clarify just one more thing. When you explain the work of the military courts, you say that they are attached to the command. Could you please explain what this word means, that they were "attached." Does that mean that they were under the command of the command that they were attached to or established, or does that mean something else?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: They are completely independent in their judicial and prosecutorial work. When you say that they're attached, it just means, it's a description saying that this command is obliged to provide conditions for this body to work unimpeded, to carry out all its requests, because it covers the territory also covered by that command. So the command is obliged to provide premises, accommodation, security, protection. This is what it means. In its actual peacetime, it is completely independent and the logistics matters are covered by the Ministry of Defence; but in wartime these technical matters are dealt with by the command where they are located, logistics including protection, premises, transport. They would make these requests to the command because there is no other organ which would be able to provide and fulfil these requests. And that is why this term is used "attached." It is not in the command and is not part of the command, and the command has no authority over this body in any kind of essential manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. I think that we could go and take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. We must break for half an hour for the tapes to be rewound, and we will continue again at five minutes past 11.00. A court officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, a few more questions about the relationship and the independence of military courts. You explained what it means to establish military courts after the proclamation of the state of war, which would then be attached to the commands. Can you please tell me what the relationship of the military courts is vis-à-vis the General Staff, what was that relationship?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: The relationship was the same. There is a certain distance. The General Staff is the highest command in the army in relationship to the military justice organs, so you would have the supreme military court in the same seat as the General Staff. But courts do not have direct contacts relating to their jurisdiction other than matters that have to do with the administration of these courts, and that was something that our legal administration dealt with. This practically means that the courts and the prosecutors were independent in making their decisions, and they are obliged only to apply the laws and regulations in effect in accordance with the law and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is perhaps just a confirmation of what you have just said, but in order to be precise, could military commanders in any way influence the work of the military courts; and based on your experience, were there such cases, such instances?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: A military commander by the very nature of their duties and functions and in view of the fact that their powers are also regulated by laws, had no authority pursuant to any law or regulation to influence the work of the court or the military prosecutors. Their only duty was to report the perpetrators of crimes to the prosecutor, and at the request of the prosecutor to obtain evidence, documents, and so on. That's where their work ended. They had no legal authority or possibility to exert any influence, so they did not do that. They could voice some desires, requests for faster processing of a specific perpetrator of a crime; they could perhaps point to this, but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This seems to be an answer that deals more with the legal aspects of the matter. Based on your experience and since in 1999 you were involved with military courts and prosecutors' offices, did you notice that anyone from the structures and the organs of the Army of Yugoslavia exerted any kind of influence or attempted to exert such an influence on the military courts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I have been in the military judicial branch for over 30 years. I've been carrying out many duties, and I have never come across such a case and did not come across any such instances during the war. There was one kind of incident at a lower level. This happened in Novi Sad, where one military senior officer submitted charges for some conscripts that did not respond to the call-up, and in order to prevent such behaviour he ordered his subordinates to take measures and to submit a report. And in that document he asked for severe punishment. When the prosecutor received that, they immediately informed the president of the supreme military court that such excesses should be prevented. On the part of the command the courts were acting pursuant to their conscience. So any kind of such behaviour was ridiculous. I mean, it was probably a senior officer without much experience. So this is the only instance in my career that spanned 30 or 40 years, where I came across such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you just described I think is mentioned in one of the documents that we will look at a bit later --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is mentioned in one overall analysis document that was drafted in order to study what experience the military courts had in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You as head of legal administration within the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, did you attempt to influence the work of the military courts or military prosecutors during that period of time, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not influence their work. I exerted no influence over their work. My duty was to assist them in doing their work without any hindrance. So I provided any assistance that I could as a colleague, assistance and support on all matters without influencing their work. I never attempted to influence anybody's work, either during peacetime or during wartime, as a president of the court or in any other capacity, because the essence of the work of judges and prosecutors is such that they need to work independently. That is the role in any legal system.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us go back to the 16th of April, 1999. You take new office on that day -- you took new office. Did you observe any problems at the time; and if so, which were those problems that you came across at the very beginning of your new position as head of legal administration within the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Based on my previous experience, I knew that whenever one assumes new office, takes new position, and comes into a new working environment, they -- and they want to be responsible in their work, they need to first take stock of the situation in that institution. As a professional with a long-standing experience, I knew the duties and obligations of every prosecutor and on every court; and I knew that there were always some deficiencies, first of all in organisational sense and also in legal technical sense. When I say "organisational," I mean that, yes, there was a certain organigram that was followed in setting up any institution, but how does one go about organise the work of any court? It can only be done by a person who is very well familiar with exact duties of the court. So it's not just a machine that you need to plug in. And as for the legal specialist kind of work, there were some issues there too. In order for somebody to work in a court, they need to have a law degree and take a bar exam and also have an officer's rank. There were situations in practice that clerks who assigned people to the post of a judge had to make sure that all those requirements are met, but they didn't necessarily always make sure that they had the necessary experience. So, for example, we had situation where somebody used to work in a bank as a lawyer and had a bar exam and had an officer's rank and was appointed to the post of a judge without any necessary experience. So naturally such people could not do their work properly because in wartime one has no time to learn how to work as a judge. So those were some of the problems and they resulted from the fact that some of the clerks who worked in those posts did not have the necessary skills or knowledge. I immediately saw this as a problem. I commenced with reorganisation of personnel, and I demanded that people be appointed to the post of a judge only with previous judicial experience or experience as a judge in other courts. And if they lacked the necessary experience of an officer, I proposed that such people be promoted in an extraordinary procedure because there was a possibility to do that under the law. And in this way, we were able to appoint proper judges, professionals who were up to the task. That was one of the first steps because without the necessary staff one could not do the job under those difficult conditions. Now, when it comes for technical problems, meaning typists, computers, technical, logistical assistance, yes, a lot of work needed to be done there, there were a lot of problems there, because the commands did not have the necessary knowledge or experience to know what needs to be done. They had never come across such tasks before. And yes, there were difficulties there, and not only the General Staff but also the lower-level commands had a lot of understanding and provided a lot of support for us in that regard. I introduced professional transcript court reporters, and we hired typists who had proper mental and physical capabilities to perform under those difficult circumstances, wartime and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of everything you have told us so far, in wartime it is -- speed can be a problem and obviously speed is of the essence here. Now, in rectifying these deficiencies, were you able to do it speedily, and were you able to correct everything in a satisfactory manner?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Realising what problems and difficulties existed -- and I was able to do that within a couple of days through my contact with the president of the Supreme Court and the prosecutor because we were all in the same location and via contacts with prosecutors and judges out there in the field, and later on I was able to tour these locations as well. So having done all that work, I was able to come up with a proposal and it was done overnight and submitted to the General Staff. And it was immediately that same evening submitted to the General Staff. They looked at it at 7.00 p.m. one evening, and on the following day in the morning I was told that a decision was taken to resolve this. And then I went further on, had contacts with prosecutors, and got in touch with the Ministry of Justice to implement this, to promote the people that were qualified, so that they could take up their posts. So yes, it was done rather quickly, and the same approach was taken with regard to technical, logistical problems. There were contacts with the military police as well and they got in touch with the people out in the field because you know that was wartime, and courts needed to have security detail and the necessary capabilities in that sense. You know, they needed to secure the detention facilities and so on. So when it comes to my proposal and the request that I sent to the General Staff, all of it was resolved in less than 24 hours. The courts and the prosecutors worked around-the-clock, except for the time when they slept, which was some four to five hours; the rest of their time was devoted to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your exhaustive answer. We just need a sort of a conclusion here. Do you think that you received full support and assistance from the General Staff that was available and possible at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We spoke about the independence of courts. Now, tell me, please, as far as you're concerned, were you independent in your work? Were you able to make decisions independently, on your own, could you make proposals about how your administration needs to function, what improvements need to be made in the judicial system, and so on, within your scope of authorities of course?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever was within my competence, whatever I could decide upon as chief of the administration, I did without any interference from anybody else. And as for my proposals that General Staff or some other organ had to rule upon, it was done immediately, without any hesitation. I did my best to make sure that my proposals were proper, rational, competent. I had enough knowledge and experience to make sure that I didn't request something that objectively could not be done. All my superiors, all superior officers acknowledged this and made sure that my requests were met as quickly and as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you believe that while you held office as chief of legal administration, military courts, military prosecutor's office, and military judicial system in general in the territory of FRY and Serbia functioned properly and met their mandate under the law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: In the given conditions and circumstances and in accordance with the optimum of their mental and physical abilities, the judicial system performed their work at an exceptionally high level. Whatever was not possible to do given the objective circumstances, they didn't do it; but whatever was up to them to carry out, they did it. And looking at the number of cases that were processed and looking at the quality of work, one is bound to give very high marks to their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we please turn to some more specific issues, issues that are of interest to everybody in this courtroom, and that is the manner in which the legal system of Serbia and Yugoslavia treated crimes against civilians and what was their attitude towards abiding by international conventions and provisions of the international laws of war? By putting this question, I first of all want you to tell us what laws regulated this area and what is it that military courts and military prosecutors relied upon in their work and as part of the laws in effect in Serbia and Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Any state should have its own ordered judicial system. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a state, a newly formed state after the preceding state, the SFRY, created all the laws and regulations also that dealt with international humanitarian law. They also covered this matter in the constitution. I think it was Article 16 of the FRY constitution which stated that all international agreements, which are ratified and published pursuant to the constitution as well as all generally accepted rules of international law, comprise an integral part of a country's internal order. I mean, this is a constitutional article that deals with this matter, which is also covered by the Geneva Convention and is also one of the tenets of the legal order of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So the Criminal Code devotes Section 16 to this matter, which provides for punishment for all of these crimes which are covered by international humanitarian law, including genocide, war crimes against civilian populations, against prisoners of war, wounded persons, and so on and so forth. So these crimes are regulated, and punishments for them are laid down. There's also a Law on Defence, which in Article 19 I think regulates cases when members of the Army of Yugoslavia who take part in combat are duty-bound in all circumstances to abide by the rules of international laws of war and other laws regulating the treatment of prisoners, wounded persons, and that cover protection of the civilian population. So on the basis of all of these laws and regulations dealing with this subject, certain instructions are also provided for members of the army, and they include everyone starting from just regular soldiers all the way up to the command, how each individual taking part in combat should behave and how they should adhere to these international norms. In case they fail to respect them, they are subject to the appropriate punishment as laid down in the law. This is precisely why military courts were formed at the level of each unit. So this was put into practice covering the organisational normative, operational, and all other aspects, so that this particular subject matter would be covered enabling the normal functioning and the respect for the laws laid down by international agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard about the legislative framework, which was in place for the application of international humanitarian law. Please tell us, in your work did you insist on a certain type of conduct on the part of the military officers in the field in terms of uncovering possible criminal offences and submission of information on such?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Let me emphasize apart from the legislative framework that at the level of the General Staff a summary was produced of all international humanitarian law provisions and rules of war and produced for each member of the VJ at different levels, the combatants, officers, at different levels; how to conduct themselves in war. Of course, the war colleges teach attendees on such matters. There were also courses at different commands and units provided for the staff. So we did conduct some training at command levels. What your question hints at is as follows: Apart from all the instructions and the regulations and the aide-memoirs and the brochures sent to unit commands, I produced a memory-jogger which summarises all legal proceedings in practice, starting from the duties of military officers, what they should do if his subordinates were to perpetrate a criminal offence, all the way to military courts. So I summarised the duties of the military officers; then investigation and detection organs, which means military police; then who receives any criminal reports; and then there was an explanation of what does -- what the military prosecutor does, what the military court does, and appeal proceedings. This was put in one place, in one brochure, which could be used by any individual to take action with respect to the criminal offence, the perpetrator of such criminal offence in respect of evidence, and the procedure to -- how to treat the detainee. And this was also done in the process of preparation so that everybody had that brochure with them so that they shouldn't wonder whether they could do something or could not, whether they should do something or not. I provided with this summary of procedural mechanisms.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. General, let's go through some documents, and for that purpose I will give you a binder of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to seek assistance from the usher. This is our standard procedure. We produced a binder of documents to facilitate the process. We just put down the numbers of documents that we are going to work on. It's not annotated in any way other than by giving -- being separated by tabs. So if you allow me, I would like to provide that binder to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, each time I'm going to announce documents to be seen in e-court, I will refer to the number of each tab. So this would be your guidance to find the relevant documents. Let's see, please, document D011-0912. That would be tab 2 in your binder, General. This is a document entitled: "Regulations of the Application of International Laws of War in the Armed Forces of the SFRY." General, my first question to you is: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you about its contents, let's take a look at the bottom of this page. It can be seen in the Serbian version, and it can be seen in the English version if we were to scroll down. The year printed there is 1988. My question to you is: Those rules on the application of international laws of war in the armed forces of the SFRY were in force in 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something more about this document. It is a voluminous document. We're not going to go into details. Briefly, whatever you can say about it, do so, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: This is a large volume containing the most salient provisions of international humanitarian and international laws of war and all other rules and customs of war as envisaged by international conventions, treaties, in a detailed but very user-friendly way. It contains an instruction prepared by the federal secretariat for national defence on the basis of an order of the president of the Presidency of SFRY, who authorised the federal secretary to prepare such an instruction, and this was done. This addition was adapted to the domestic legal order. It had existed beforehand. It still applies, but of course there are different provisions within laws and the constitution who govern such issues. This contains Geneva Conventions, international humanitarian law. The contents have not been changed because no other international conventions have been brought into force to modify or amend the erstwhile conventions. It was in force then and this volume was used for training, for educating our officers at war schools, at military schools, and of course it was in force in the VJ, and it was part of the internal legal order of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and then in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and today in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I believe this document may already be in evidence as a Prosecution exhibit, P1342. Perhaps this can be checked just to avoid duplication of documents in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will leave the matter of its admission, Mr. Popovic, until that can be resolved. Perhaps you can look at it over the next break if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honours. Thank you. And I would like to thank my learned colleague. We will check the documents already admitted. Thank you. Now let's see D011-1132.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That would be tab 3 in your binder, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: On the screen you can see this document entitled: "Rules of Conduct For Soldiers." Please tell us, first of all, whether you are familiar with this document and after that what you can briefly tell us about what it constituted, who the target audience was, and who received it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. The staff of the Supreme Command prepared it, and it contains the most important rules for conduct for combatants, and "combatant" is an international law term. This was delivered to each and every soldier, and it summarises the duties and the rule of conduct for combatants in combat. For instance, there are rules of combat briefly: Fight only against soldiers, attack only military targets, treat people, et cetera, et cetera, this -- these are the rules derived from the rules of combat. Then we have treatment of wounded enemy soldiers, what treatment they should be given. Then treatment of prisoners of war and treatment of civilians, in keeping with international humanitarian law. We can see four pages here. It is a pocket-sized volume. It was printed on plastified paper, which means it's water and humidity resistant, and each soldier received one copy. Whenever they were called up, this was part of the equipment they were given, together with a helmet, a rifle, a first aid kit, and this was part and parcel of the regular issue equipment. Each soldier was familiar with this document.
